## DRAIN-CYCLE PROJECT ANALYSIS

### 1. WHAT IT IS

**Language & Type:** Python 3.11+ CLI tool installed via `uv tool install`

**Entry Point:** `drain-cycle` command (via `/Users/anton/src/drain-cycle/drain_cycle/cli.py` → `main()`)

**README Summary:** Unattended execution of a Linear cycle — one invocation, no prompts; spawns fresh `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` sessions per issue in isolated git worktrees. Each worker independently marks its issue Done in Linear upon completion. The orchestrator monitors each spawn and halts the run on the first non-Done exit. Tools exist for status monitoring, grading run health across cycles, and per-ticket outcome verification.

---

### 2. HOW IT ORCHESTRATES

**Architecture:**
- **Orchestrator** (`drain_cycle/orchestrator.py`): Main loop that fetches the current Linear cycle, topologically sorts Todo/Backlog issues (respecting blocks/blocked-by), and spawns one worker per issue sequentially
- **Per-Issue Worker** (`drain_cycle/worker.py`): Spawns `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` with `--output-format stream-json --verbose`, parses token usage on the wire, monitors token/time breaches, SIGKILLs on guardrail violation
- **Linear Client** (`drain_cycle/linear.py`): Direct GraphQL queries to `https://api.linear.app/graphql` (no SDK); resolves current cycle, fetches pending issues, fetches issue state, transitions issues Todo→In Progress and agent-driven → Done

**Work Selection:**
- Linear cycle concept: operator defines current cycle in Linear with issues, blocks/dependencies, labels
- Issue resolution order: topological sort via Kahn's algorithm respecting blocks; ties broken by `(sortOrder, id)` (operator's manual drag order)
- Label-driven routing:
  - `repo:<name>` → maps to target repo path via `~/.drain-cycle/repos.yml`
  - `model:<alias>` → overrides worker model (default `claude-sonnet-4-6`); aliases: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`
  - `verify` → switches to verify-flow pipeline (Task Shaper preamble + outcome verification pre-Done)

**The Loop:**
1. **Pick issue** (next topologically-ready Todo/Backlog)
2. **Setup**: Create `.worktrees/<issue-id>/` branched off `main`; symlink project config (`.claude/`, `.mcp.json`, optionally `.entire/`) into worktree
3. **Transition**: Move issue Todo → In Progress via Linear GraphQL (orchestrator-owned, happens before spawn)
4. **Spawn worker**: `claude -p` in worktree with prompt (title + description + instructions + tail)
5. **Worker loop**: Agent reads issue, implements, reviews (via `/code-review-and-quality`), commits, pushes, marks Done via Linear MCP
6. **Monitor**: Parse stream-json for token usage; SIGKILL on per-issue time/token cap breach
7. **Verify**: Re-fetch issue state post-exit; if not Done → halt run, preserve worktree; if Done → remove worktree, move to next issue
8. **Cycle guard**: After each Done, check cycle-wide caps; stop run if breached

**Resume Pattern:** On re-run, if a worktree for an issue already exists, reuse it (bounded by `max_resume_attempts`); prompt includes `_resume_directive` telling agent to `git log main..HEAD` first.

---

### 3. INTEGRATION POINTS

**Linear Integration:**
- **Mechanism**: Direct GraphQL client (httpx), no SDK
- **Reads**:
  - Current cycle via `CurrentCycle` query (hardcoded team `Personal`)
  - Pending issues (Todo/Backlog) via `CyclePending` query; flattens `labels { nodes { name parent { name } } }` → `labels: list[str]`; extracts `inverseRelations` with `type == "blocks"` → `blockers: [{id, identifier, state_type}]`
  - Issue state refresh via `Issue` query (for halt detection)
  - Workflow state resolution via `WorkflowStates` query (for state transitions)
- **Writes**:
  - `issueUpdate` mutation to transition state (Todo → In Progress, In Progress → Done)
  - Agent also writes via MCP `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue` (agent-self-update pattern; decision §1)
- **Config**: `LINEAR_API_KEY` from environment (first hit: shell export → `~/.drain-cycle/.env` → repo `.env`)

**Git Integration:**
- **Mechanism**: `git worktree add`, branch checkout, `git log`, `git status`
- **Pattern**: Per-issue worktree at `.worktrees/<issue-id>`, branched off `main`; agent commits and pushes to `main`; worktree removed on Done (or preserved on halt)
- **Config**: `.gitignore` must include `.worktrees/` to prevent spawn sessions from staging the worktree dir itself

**Graphite (gt CLI):**
- **Mechanism**: Optional stack-mode uses `.drain-handoff.json` to pass PR metadata to external assembler (not yet fully integrated)
- **Config**: `mcp__graphite__run_gt_cmd` is allowlisted but not invoked in core flow (future integration point)

**MCP/Skills Exposure to Workers:**
- Workers inherit project-scoped `.claude/settings.json` (including hooks) and `.mcp.json` via symlink (design decision §10)
- Agents are expected to invoke: `/code-review-and-quality` (skill), `/shape:task` (on verify-flow), Linear MCP (`mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue`, `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_comment`)
- **See `.claude/settings.local.json`**: allowlist includes `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__*` (save_issue, save_comment, etc.) and is curated for drain-cycle workers

---

### 4. WHERE SKILLS PLUG IN

**Current Integration Points:**

1. **In Prompt Template** (`drain_cycle/prompt.py`):
   - **Normal flow tail**: `"run /code-review-and-quality on the working-tree changes, fix Critical/Required findings, commit + push, then post a review-summary comment on the issue and transition to Done"`
   - **Stack mode tail**: Same but commit without pushing; write `.drain-handoff.json` instead
   - **Verify flow preamble**: `"if verify label present, check for Task Shaper output block in issue body; if present use it, if absent run /shape:task {identifier} first"`

2. **Skills Referenced (Not Yet Integrated):**
   - `/shape:task` — invoked in verify-flow (mentioned in AGENTS.md, code hooks are there, not yet fully wired for decision)
   - `/code-review-and-quality` — invoked in all flows before Done
   - Planned (from `docs/initiative-multi-agent-collaboration.md`): `/shape:verify-implementation`, `/shape:pr-prepare`, `/shape:pr-respond`

3. **What The Prompt Expects:**
   - Issue **title** and **body** (description) — exact text from Linear
   - **Working directory**: `{worktree_path}`
   - **Base branch**: `main`
   - **Explicit sequence** (in normal flow):
     1. Run `/code-review-and-quality` against changes
     2. Fix Critical/Required findings
     3. Commit and push to main
     4. Post review-summary comment via `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_comment`
     5. Transition to Done via `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue`

4. **Acceptance Criteria Format Expected:**
   - Issue **description** is passed verbatim to the prompt; no special parsing of AC format
   - Agents read and interpret AC; no manifest files (no `.drain.yml` or similar in issue body yet)

5. **Verify Flow Specifics** (from `drain_cycle/prompt.py`):
   - Check for `<!-- TASK-SHAPER-START -->` / `<!-- TASK-SHAPER-END -->` block in issue body
   - If present, use it; if absent, invoke `/shape:task {identifier}` and use output
   - Then proceed with normal implementation flow

---

### 5. CURRENT STATE: COMPLETENESS & DIRECTION

**Implemented & Shipped:**
- ✅ US-A: Unattended cycle drain (core loop, one worker per issue sequentially)
- ✅ US-B: Halt inspection (worktree preservation, run-log entry with halt_reason)
- ✅ US-C: Run-log artefacts (JSON logs per cycle at `~/.drain-cycle/runs/<cycle-id>-<run-timestamp>.json`)

**Planned / In Design Phase:**
- 🚧 **Verify-flow multi-agent pipeline** (`docs/initiative-multi-agent-collaboration.md`, `flow.py` skeleton present):
  - Task Shaper (`/shape:task`) — verify-flow preamble calls it; decision output stored in issue body

**Design Documents:**

**Test Coverage:**

**Known Kill Conditions:**
- Dependency cycle in blocks graph → immediate halt with issue list
- Missing `repo:<name>` label → per-issue halt before spawn
- External unresolved blocker → deferred (not run, not logged)
- Issue still In Progress after worker exit → halt + revert To Todo if resume cap reached
- Per-issue token/time/cost breach → halt + SIGKILL worker
- Cycle-wide breach → halt + preserve worktree of issue that caused it

## SYNTHESIS FOR SKILL PACK INTEGRATION

If you're building skills to integrate with `drain-cycle`:

1. **Invoke pattern**: Skills are called via `/skill-name` in the prompt (no slash-command system in drain-cycle itself, only in spawned agents). Agents inherit global and project-scoped skills via Claude Code's normal discovery.

2. **Handoff pattern**: For verify-flow, the `/shape:task` output is stored in the issue body inside HTML comments; downstream agents (implementer, verifier) read it. For stack mode, `.drain-handoff.json` is the inter-agent contract.

3. **Linear integration**: Agents use MCP (`mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue`, `mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_comment`) to update issues; orchestrator sees the state change and decides halt vs. continue.

4. **Run-log visibility**: The orchestrator records per-issue token usage, cost, exit code, and halt_reason. Skills that want to be graded must surface their verdict (pass/fail) in ways the agent can encode back to Linear (comment, issue state, or in the reach of `grade-draft`).

5. **Project config symlink**: Skills in `.claude/agents/` or registered in `.claude/settings.json` hooks are automatically available in worker worktrees via the symlink; no special registration needed beyond what you'd do for interactive Claude Code use.

## 2. Lifecycle coverage and chaining

Full idea→ship coverage, explicitly mapped in `using-agent-skills/SKILL.md` ("Lifecycle Sequence", 15 steps):
interview-me → idea-refine → spec-driven-development → planning-and-task-breakdown → context-engineering → source-driven-development → incremental-implementation → doubt-driven-development → test-driven-development → code-review-and-quality → code-simplification → git-workflow-and-versioning → documentation-and-adrs → deprecation-and-migration → shipping-and-launch.

Artifact chain (file-based, repo-committed):
- `/spec` → `SPEC.md` (project root), human-approved before advancing.
- `/plan` reads SPEC.md → `tasks/plan.md` + `tasks/todo.md`.
- `/build` reads the plan, executes one task at a time, marks tasks complete — this is the spec → plan → build loop.
- spec-driven-development itself is a 4-phase gated pipeline (SPECIFY → PLAN → TASKS → IMPLEMENT) with a human review gate between each phase, and Phase 4 explicitly delegates to incremental-implementation + test-driven-development + context-engineering by file path.
- Sequential pipeline is *user-driven*: the agents/README decision matrix says dependent steps run as "Sequential slash commands run by the user (/spec → /plan → /build → /test → /review)" — no autonomous pipeline runner.

## 3. Sub-agent derivatives

- Definition format: minimal frontmatter — only `name` + `description`. **No `tools`, no `model` field** in any of the three. Body is a pure role/system prompt: role statement, review scope, severity scheme, mandatory output template, numbered Rules, and a closing **"Composition" block** (Invoke directly when / Invoke via / "Do not invoke from another persona").
- Three-layer doctrine (agents/README.md): Skill = the *how*, Persona = the *who* (perspective + output format), Command = the *when* (composition). Hard rule: personas never call personas — orchestration belongs to slash commands or the user; noted as also platform-enforced ("subagents cannot spawn other subagents").
- How skills/commands reference them: `/ship` Phase A issues three Agent tool calls "in a single assistant turn" with `subagent_type: code-reviewer|security-auditor|test-engineer`. `/review` wraps code-reviewer alone; `/test` wraps test-engineer. Persona resolution: user-level `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/` definitions deliberately override the plugin versions.
- `references/orchestration-patterns.md` catalogs 5 endorsed patterns (direct invocation, single-persona command, parallel fan-out + merge, user-driven sequential pipeline, research isolation), an explicit anti-pattern (meta-orchestrator routing persona — "pure routing layer, 2x token cost"), and Claude Code interop notes: Agent Teams (experimental, persona body appended to teammate prompt), and a warning that plugin agents silently ignore `hooks`, `mcpServers`, `permissionMode` frontmatter.

## 4. Authoring style

- Length: skills 178–390 lines, median ~290. Commands ~15–20 lines (ship is the outlier at 72). Agents ~95–100.
- Frontmatter: only `name` + `description` (max 1024 chars; "what in third person + 'Use when' triggers; never summarize the workflow in the description or the agent follows the summary instead of the skill").
- Canonical section pattern (`docs/skill-anatomy.md`): Title → Overview → When to Use (incl. when NOT) → Core Process/Workflow → Techniques/Patterns → **Common Rationalizations** (excuse | reality table — called "the most distinctive feature") → **Red Flags** → **Verification** (evidence-backed exit checklist). Recommended, not rigid.
- Tone: imperative second-person, anti-rationalization, ASCII flowcharts/diagrams, concrete commands ("Run `npm test`" beats "verify tests"), TypeScript/npm-flavored examples throughout (notably *not* stack-agnostic — code snippets assume Node/React/Prisma). Writing principles: process over knowledge, specific over general, evidence over assumption, token-conscious, progressive disclosure.
- Behavioral spine in using-agent-skills: surface assumptions ("Correct me now or I'll proceed"), stop on confusion, push back (anti-sycophancy), enforce simplicity, scope discipline, verify-don't-assume.

## 5. Delivery/execution specifics

**/build** (`.claude/commands/build.md`): invokes incremental-implementation + test-driven-development together. Per-task loop: read AC → load context → failing test (RED) → minimum code (GREEN) → full suite → build → commit → mark complete → next. Failure routes to debugging-and-error-recovery. The underlying skill adds: Increment Cycle (Implement→Test→Verify→Commit→next slice), three slicing strategies (vertical preferred, contract-first, risk-first), Rule 0 Simplicity First, Rule 0.5 Scope Discipline ("NOTICED BUT NOT TOUCHING" pattern), keep-compilable, feature flags for incomplete work, rollback-friendly increments, ~100-line-before-test red flag, and an anti-redundant-verification rule (don't rerun unchanged builds).

**/ship**: three-phase orchestrator. Phase A — parallel fan-out, all three Agent calls in one turn ("sequential calls defeat the purpose"); fallback for non-Claude harnesses is sequential invocation treated as parallel. Phase B — merge in main context across 6 axes (quality, security, performance, accessibility, infrastructure, docs); accessibility/infra/docs handled directly by main agent since no persona covers them. Phase C — GO/NO-GO template with Blockers / Recommended fixes / Acknowledged risks / mandatory Rollback plan (trigger conditions, procedure, RTO) / full specialist reports appended. Rules: any persona Critical ⇒ default NO-GO unless user accepts risk; skip fan-out only if ≤2 files AND <50 lines AND no auth/payments/data/config touch.

**Verification model**: every skill ends in a Verification checklist requiring evidence (test output, build result, screenshot); tasks carry explicit AC + verification commands; checkpoints every 2–3 tasks in plans; shipping-and-launch adds quantified rollout thresholds (advance/hold/rollback table, e.g. error rate >2x baseline ⇒ rollback) and a first-hour post-launch routine. browser-testing-with-devtools provides runtime verification via Chrome DevTools MCP.

**Git/PR handling**: git-workflow-and-versioning — trunk-based, main always deployable, 1–3-day feature branches, conventional commits, ~100 lines/commit-or-PR target, split >1000, worktrees for parallel streams, refactor/feature separation. Notably **no PR mechanics**: no `gh pr create`, no PR-body authoring, no merge/auto-merge policy, no stacked PRs. `/build` commits but never branches, pushes, or opens PRs.

## 6. Gaps

- **No tracker integration** — no Linear/Jira/GitHub-Issues concept; plans live as `tasks/*.md` files; no issue lifecycle, no status updates.
- **No PR preparation/merge workflow** — commit discipline yes; PR creation, descriptions, review-routing, auto-merge, stacking: absent.
- **No product layer** — no triage/prioritization/scoring (ICE/Kano), no roadmap or capacity planning, no initiative/OKR shaping, no kill conditions or appetite. interview-me/idea-refine are the only upstream-of-spec artifacts and they target a single feature idea.
- **No estimation/sizing beyond XS–XL file-count buckets**; no model-tier routing of tasks; no delegation/breakdown-at-pickup concept.
- **No autonomous pipeline** — spec→plan→build→ship gates all require the human to invoke each command; no end-to-end runner.
- **No incident response / observability operations** — monitoring is set up at launch, but no debugging-in-production, on-call, postmortem skill.
- **No data/ML, infra-as-code, database-design, or release-versioning (semver/changelog automation) skills.**
- **Stack drift vs stated agnosticism** — examples are uniformly TypeScript/npm/React/Prisma; the checklists (CWV, bundle size, axe-core) assume web frontend.
- **Spike/prototype path missing** — risk-first slicing exists, but no throwaway-prototype or research-spike artifact with a proceed/kill verdict.
- **Verification is self-attested** — checklists, not deterministic hooks; the only enforcement hooks shipped are SessionStart injection, the SDD WebFetch cache, and simplify-ignore redaction (no diff-scanning gate like stop-the-line).

## 2. Lifecycle coverage and chaining

**Covered stages:** idea → design/spec → plan → execute → per-task review → finish (merge/PR). Plus orthogonal disciplines: TDD, debugging, verification, review reception.

**The canonical chain (each skill explicitly names the next as "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL"):**

```
brainstorming
  → writes spec to docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md
  → user-approval gate → invokes writing-plans (the ONLY allowed next skill)
writing-plans
  → writes plan to docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature>.md
  → plan header itself embeds: "REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: use subagent-driven-development
    (recommended) or executing-plans"
  → offers user choice: Subagent-Driven vs Inline
subagent-driven-development | executing-plans
  → both require using-git-worktrees first (isolated workspace)
  → per task: TDD (subagents told to follow it), requesting-code-review templates
  → both terminate by invoking finishing-a-development-branch
finishing-a-development-branch
  → merge locally | push + PR | keep | discard (+ worktree cleanup)
```

**Cross-cutting:** `verification-before-completion` fires before any "done/fixed/passing" claim; `systematic-debugging` fires on any bug before fixes (links into TDD Phase 4); `receiving-code-review` mediates feedback; `using-superpowers` is the SessionStart router that makes skill invocation compulsory (including a graph node forcing brainstorming before EnterPlanMode). `using-superpowers` also encodes priority: process skills (brainstorming, debugging) before implementation skills.

**Notable mechanism:** the lifecycle handoff lives in artifacts, not just skills — the plan document header tells *future agents in fresh sessions* which skill to use. Checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax in plans serves as cross-session progress tracking.

## 3. Sub-agent usage

Three distinct patterns:

**A. One-subagent-per-task with two-stage review loop** (`subagent-driven-development`):
- Controller reads the plan once, extracts ALL tasks with full text upfront; subagents are *never* told to read the plan file ("Make subagent read plan file" is a listed red flag).
- Per task: dispatch implementer (general-purpose Task tool, `implementer-prompt.md`) → implementer can ask questions *before and during* work → implements + tests + commits + self-reviews → dispatch **spec compliance reviewer** → then (only after spec ✅) **code quality reviewer** → reviewer-found issues go back to the *same* implementer, then re-review. Strict ordering: quality review before spec compliance passes is a named red flag.
- Implementer status protocol: `DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT`, with controller playbook per status (BLOCKED → more context / more capable model / split task / escalate to human).
- **Model routing built in:** mechanical 1–2-file tasks → cheap model; integration → standard; architecture/review → most capable.
- Spec reviewer prompt contains a deliberate distrust framing: "The implementer finished suspiciously quickly. Their report may be incomplete... DO NOT take their word." Verify by reading code, not the report.
- Never dispatch multiple *implementation* subagents in parallel (conflict risk); continuous execution with no "should I continue?" check-ins.
- After all tasks: one final whole-implementation reviewer, then finishing-a-development-branch.

**B. Parallel investigation agents** (`dispatching-parallel-agents`): one agent per independent problem domain (e.g. 3 unrelated failing test files), dispatched concurrently; prompts must be focused, self-contained, constrained ("Do NOT change production code"), with specified return format; controller verifies no conflicts + runs full suite after.

**C. Reviewer-as-subagent** (`requesting-code-review`): dispatch a "Senior Code Reviewer" persona with `{DESCRIPTION, PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS, BASE_SHA, HEAD_SHA}`; reviews the git diff range, returns Strengths / Issues (Critical/Important/Minor) / Recommendations / "Ready to merge? Yes|No|With fixes".

**Shared philosophy (stated identically in both subagent skills):** subagents never inherit session context/history — the controller hand-crafts exactly the context they need; this both keeps them focused and preserves the controller's context for coordination. Worktree isolation is a *prerequisite of the workflow* (via using-git-worktrees), not per-subagent — subagents share the one worktree, serialized.

## 4. Authoring style

- **Frontmatter: just two fields** — `name` and `description`. No version, author, length targets, or taxonomy. Descriptions are trigger-condition-shaped, third person: "Use when X, before Y - does Z" (some add intensity: brainstorming's starts "You MUST use this before any creative work").
- **Length:** 70–371 lines for workflow skills (median ~190); writing-skills is the outlier at 655. The pack's own guidance (writing-skills): keep sections <150 lines, SKILL.md <200 lines preferred, push details to companion files in the skill dir loaded on demand (progressive disclosure).
- **Recurring structural devices:**
  - **"Iron Law" blocks** — single-sentence absolutes in code fences (TDD, verification, debugging) plus "Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule."
  - **Graphviz `dot` digraphs** as machine-readable flowcharts for decision logic and process loops (brainstorming, subagent-driven, using-superpowers, dispatching-parallel, TDD). There's a whole `graphviz-conventions.dot` style guide.
  - **Rationalization tables** (Excuse | Reality two-column) — explicitly designed to pre-empt the agent's own excuses ("I'm confident" → "Confidence ≠ evidence"; "Emergency, no time" → "Systematic is FASTER").
  - **Red Flags sections** — "Never:" / "Always:" bullet lists, or thought-pattern tables ("if you catch yourself thinking X, STOP").
  - **Quick Reference tables** (situation → action).
  - **Common Mistakes** with Problem/Fix pairs.
  - **Announce-at-start lines**: "I'm using the X skill to Y" — makes skill use observable to the human.
  - **Checklists mapped to TodoWrite** (brainstorming mandates a todo per checklist item; using-superpowers's flowchart enforces this generally).
  - ✅/❌ contrastive example pairs for behavioral patterns.
  - Concrete worked example transcripts (subagent-driven has a full 70-line simulated session).
  - "Real-World Impact" sections citing session data ("first-time fix rate 95% vs 40%", "from 24 failure memories").
- **Tone:** imperative, absolutist, anti-rationalization; moralized stakes ("Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency"; "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced"). Persuasion is deliberate — `writing-skills/persuasion-principles.md` documents the influence techniques used. Addresses the user as "your human partner" throughout.
- **What makes them effective/terse:** every section is either a gate, a table, a flowchart, or a prompt template — almost no expository filler; exact bash commands with expected output; deterministic decision tables (e.g. finishing-a-development-branch's environment-detection table keyed on `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`); skills are *tested* — writing-skills mandates TDD-for-docs with subagent pressure-testing (`testing-skills-with-subagents.md`, `test-pressure-*.md` fixtures) before deployment.
- **Distribution trick:** the SessionStart hook injects the entire `using-superpowers` skill into context wrapped in `<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>`, making the dispatcher always-loaded while everything else stays lazy.

## 5. Delivery/execution capabilities in detail

**executing-plans (inline mode, 70 lines — deliberately thin):** load plan → critical review (raise concerns before starting) → TodoWrite per task → follow steps *exactly* → run specified verifications → finishing-a-development-branch. Stop conditions: blocker, critical plan gap, unclear instruction, repeated verification failure — "ask rather than guess." The skill itself says: if subagents are available, use subagent-driven-development instead. Never start on main/master without explicit consent.

**subagent-driven-development:** see §3A. Key delivery properties: continuous autonomous execution (the README claims multi-hour autonomous runs), per-task commit discipline (implementer commits within the task), review loops that must re-run until ✅, controller never fixes code manually ("context pollution" — dispatch a fix subagent instead).

**Verification model — three reinforcing layers:**
1. *Plan-level:* every plan step embeds its own verification command + expected output ("Run: pytest ... Expected: FAIL with 'function not defined'"); TDD red-green is baked into the step template.
2. *Task-level:* implementer self-review checklist (completeness/quality/discipline/testing) + two independent reviewer subagents reading actual code/diffs, not reports.
3. *Claim-level:* verification-before-completion's gate function (IDENTIFY command → RUN fresh → READ full output → VERIFY → only then claim) applies to any success claim, including "Agent completed" (requires checking VCS diff, never trusting the agent's report) and regression tests (require demonstrated red-green: pass → revert fix → must fail → restore → pass).

**Git/branches/PRs:**
- Isolation first: using-git-worktrees runs before execution. Detection order: already-isolated check (`GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, with submodule guard) → native harness tool (EnterWorktree etc. — "the #1 mistake" is using raw git when a native tool exists) → manual `git worktree add` under `.worktrees/` (must verify gitignored, commit .gitignore change) → sandbox fallback to in-place. Then auto setup (npm/cargo/pip/go) + clean baseline test run before any work.
- Commits: frequent, per plan step ("Step 5: Commit" with exact `git add`/`git commit` commands in the plan).
- Finishing: tests must pass before options are even presented; exactly 4 options (3 on detached HEAD — no local merge). PR path: `git push -u origin` + `gh pr create` with Summary + Test Plan body; worktree preserved for PR iteration. Merge path: merge → re-run tests on merged result → only then remove worktree → delete branch (ordering prevents `branch -d` failure). Discard requires the user to type the literal word "discard". Cleanup respects provenance: only remove worktrees superpowers created (`.worktrees/`, `worktrees/`, `~/.config/superpowers/worktrees/`); harness-owned workspaces are left alone. Never force-push without explicit request.

## 6. Gaps — what it does NOT cover

- **No product/portfolio layer:** nothing upstream of "an idea arrives" — no idea triage/scoring, prioritization, roadmapping, capacity planning, OKR/initiative shaping, or appetite/kill conditions. Brainstorming assumes the decision to build is already made.
- **No issue-tracker integration:** no Linear/Jira/GitHub-Issues lifecycle, no cycle/backlog governance. State lives entirely in markdown plan files + checkboxes + git.
- **No multi-PR / stacked-delivery model:** one branch, one plan, one finish. No PR stacking, no auto-merge policy, no PR-body conventions beyond a minimal template, no release/versioning/changelog/deploy skills.
- **No CI/CD, ops, or post-ship coverage:** no pipeline authoring, monitoring/observability, incident response, rollback, feature flags, or post-launch evidence loops.
- **No estimation/sizing/scheduling:** tasks are "bite-sized" by fiat; no sizing rubric, no dependency-graph or critical-path planning, no parallel execution of *implementation* tasks (explicitly forbidden — execution is strictly serial; parallelism is reserved for independent investigations).
- **No security/performance/accessibility specialist reviews:** the code-reviewer template mentions security/scalability as bullet points but there are no dedicated skills.
- **No frontend/design, data, or domain-specific engineering skills** in this plugin (README references frontend-design/mcp-builder as things brainstorming must NOT invoke — they live elsewhere).
- **No documentation/ADR skill** beyond the spec and plan artifacts; no human-facing rendering of artifacts.
- **Thin requirements rigor:** specs have a self-review (placeholders/consistency/ambiguity) but no acceptance-criteria formalism, no measurable success criteria, no adversarial plan review by an independent agent (plan review is a self-checklist; note `writing-plans/plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md` and `brainstorming/spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md` exist as templates but the SKILL.md flow uses inline self-review).
- **Minimal frontmatter/metadata:** no versioning, provenance, principle citations, or length governance fields per skill — conventions are enforced by prose in writing-skills, not by schema.

## 4. SUB-AGENT USAGE & AGENT FILES

### Agent files present

**Location**: `/Users/anton/src/agent-skills-shaper/agents/`

**1 agent defined:**

| Agent | File | Lines | Model | Review Target | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| code-reviewer | agents/code-reviewer/AGENT.md | 131 | Frontier | implementation | Multi-axis review (correctness, readability, architecture, security, performance); fires before commit to main |

**Sub-agent design:**
- **Review posture**: Adversarial; assumes at least one finding
- **Context loading**: eng-principles (universal + agentic) + spec + task-sizing rubric → form independent view before reading diff
- **Trigger**: Before issue transition to Done (per Workflow pack) OR before commit
- **Structural bias detection**:
  - Green-test victory (tests passed ≠ behaviour correct)
  - Exciting-over-boring (novel pattern vs. boring default)
  - Scope creep normalised (out-of-boundary touches)
  - Silenced signals (type casts, lint suppressions, `.skip`, deleted assertions)
- **Output**: Structured verdict (accept / accept-with-notes / reject) with findings by severity (Critical/Required/Suggested/Note)

**Dispatch mechanism**: Invoked by Workflow pack governance procedure; not explicitly called by any skill. Agent is a persistent review gate, not a skill output.

### Sub-agent dispatching within skills

**grep result**: Only `plan-review` mentions sub-agent (in description, not invocation). No skills call agents programmatically. Agents/skills are loaded separately; no skill → agent dispatch.

### Agents directory structure

```
agents/
├── code-reviewer/
│   └── AGENT.md      (131 lines)
```

No other agent files or subdirectories. **Agents are simple files, not nested structures.**

## 5. TOOL COUPLINGS & TRACKER BINDING

### Tracker agnosticism pattern

**initiative-shape** is the canonical example:

```yaml
# From initiative-shape/SKILL.md, Step 7:
- **Tracker binding installed** — if a tracker-capture procedure is loaded 
  (e.g. the Workflow pack, plugin `workflow`, whose `GOVERNANCE.md` / 
  capture procedure loads at session start and defines how this workspace 
  records initiatives in its tracker): follow that procedure. Hand it the 
  confirmed six-field shape...
- **No tracker binding** — emit the confirmed shape as the markdown block 
  in the next section, filled in, for the user to paste into whatever 
  tracker they use.
```

**Implementation**: 
- Step 7 checks for bound procedure in session context
- If bound: delegates recording to procedure (Workflow pack owns tracker calls)
- If not bound: emits markdown template for manual entry
- KR sub-field requirements (baseline/target/measured-over/how-we-know) are defined **inline** in the skill, not in tracker schema

**Tool references in skills:**

| Reference | Count | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| Linear (explicit) | 1 | initiative-shape (mentions Linear document as research source in References) |
| Workflow pack (plugin) | 5 | initiative-shape, delivery-shape, code-reviewer (agent), README |
| BigQuery / observability | 1 | initiative-shape (example in `how-we'll-know` field format) |
| MCP data sources | 2 | app-calibrate (Extension section), README |
| Git | 0 (no git coupling in skills) | — |

**Graphite**: No references found.

**Tracker binding architecture**:
- Shaper skills are **tracker-read and tracker-write naive**
- Workflow pack (separate plugin) provides tracker I/O and cycle/ops-slot model
- Shaper emits markdown shapes that are paste-ready or handed off to tracker procedures
- Principle: skills are durable, trackers are swappable

## 7. STRUCTURAL CONVENTIONS

### Required sections per skill (from docs/skill-anatomy.md)

**Frontmatter** (YAML, required):
```yaml
name: <skill-name>
description: <1-2 sentences, includes trigger phrases>
pack: <product | engineering | meta>
lifecycle_stage: <define | plan | build | ship | verify | review | meta | reference>
principles_implemented:
  - source: <eng-universal | eng-agentic | roadmap | product>
    id: <principle or rule id>
    bucket: <embedded | standalone | hook | sub-agent>
length_target: <e.g. 200-280>
author: Anton Babushkin
predecessor:
  repo: <URL or "none">
  skill: <skill name in source repo, or "none">
  relation: <derivative | adjacent | new>
kept_from_predecessor: <list, or "n/a">
changed_from_predecessor: <list, or "n/a">
```

**Body sections** (in exact order, numbered):
1. **Title** — `# <Skill Name>`
2. **Purpose** — one paragraph (load-bearing section)
3. **When to use** — explicit trigger phrases + size-the-work rubric where relevant
4. **When not to use** — explicit non-triggers, alternatives named
5. **Inputs** — what the skill expects
6. **Outputs** — deliverables, artefact paths
7. **Workflow** — numbered steps; hard gates marked `[GATE]`
8. **Artefact template** — markdown the skill produces
9. **Common rationalisations** — table of excuses + rebuttals
10. **Red flags** — bullet list of violations
11. **Verification / exit criteria** — how to know the skill ran correctly
12. **References** — citations to rules, references/, source principles

**Length target**: 100–300 lines (hard cap 350; beyond that, split)

**Meta-pack exemptions**: Skills with `pack: meta` exempt from:
- `principles_implemented` frontmatter
- `predecessor` frontmatter
- Inputs, Outputs, Artefact template, Common rationalisations, Red flags, Verification sections
- Must still have: Title, Purpose, When to use, When not to use, References

### Hook anatomy (from docs/hook-anatomy.md)

**Frontmatter**:
```yaml
name: <hook-name>
description: <1-2 sentences>
category: hook
pack: <product | engineering | meta>
trigger_event: <pr | commit | ...>
principles_implemented:
  - source: <...>
    id: <...>
    bucket: hook
length_target: <60–100>
author: Anton Babushkin
```

**Sections**:
1. Purpose
2. Trigger event
3. Check (patterns and logic)
4. Fail criteria
5. Pass criteria
6. On fail (action required)
7. Out of scope
8. References

**Length**: 60–100 lines (observed: stop-the-line 80, ta[REDACTED_SK] 85)

### Sub-agent anatomy (from docs/sub-agent-anatomy.md)

**Frontmatter** includes `model: <Fast|Balanced|Frontier>` (required)

**Sections**:
1. Purpose
2. Review posture
3. Context to load (before seeing original work)
4. Trigger
5. Inputs
6. Outputs
7. Workflow
8. Common rationalisations
9. Red flags
10. Out of scope
11. References

**Length**: 150–200 lines (hard cap 250)

**Model tier rule**: 
- `Fast` (Haiku 4.5) — mechanical leaf, enumerable pass/fail
- `Balanced` (Sonnet 4.6) — focused worker, one bounded review lane
- `Frontier` (Opus 4.7) — orchestrating review, integrates findings, propagates to downstream decisions

## 8. EXECUTION CAPABILITIES INVENTORY

### Skills explicitly addressing execution

| Skill | Lifecycle | Function | Completeness |
|---|---|---|---|
| **pr-prepare** | ship | Writes PR context (What/Why/Focus); routes to auto-merge or human review per carve-out rule | **Partial** — prep only, not review verdict; auto-merge rule is calibrated (≤200 lines, no critical signals, empty focus, CI green) |
| **verify-implementation** | verify | Maps AC items against diff; emits binary pass/fail verdict | **Partial** — outcome gate only; does not verify correctness of AC itself, only whether diff satisfies the AC that exists |
| **code-reviewer** (agent) | review | Multi-axis review (correctness, readability, architecture, security, performance) | **Partial** — review gate before merge, not during implementation; fires after work is claimed done |

### Hooks supporting execution

| Hook | Function | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| **stop-the-line** | Catches type suppressions, compiler directives, test skips, deleted assertions in PR diffs | Prevents signal suppression; does not fix root cause |
| **ta[REDACTED_SK]** | Flags tasks lacking Model: routing annotation | Ensures tasks have plan-time review-attention routing; does not verify planning correctness |

### What Shaper does NOT cover (by design)

**BUILD phase** (delegated to execution pack):
- Incremental implementation
- Test-driven development
- Debugging and error recovery
- Technical decision-making in-flight
- Code review (only: context-writing and post-implementation verification)

**DEPLOY phase**:
- Rollout strategies
- Monitoring and alerting
- Kill switches and fast rollback
- Canary analysis

**POST-LAUNCH**:
- Outcome measurement and grading against KRs
- Launch retrospectives
- DORA metrics capture

**Execution story completeness**: ~40% (PR context + outcome gate + pre-ship sub-agent review; no build/deploy/post-launch)

## 9. SUPPORTING INFRASTRUCTURE

### Session Start hook (hooks/session-start.sh)

**Mechanism**:
1. Fires on every session start
2. Loads `using-this-pack/SKILL.md` (the meta-skill)
3. Displays it as an IMPORTANT priority message
4. User sees skill discovery flowchart first

**Rationale**: Lazy-loading of all principle files; the agent discovers which rule to read based on task, not pre-loads all.

### Commands infrastructure

All 14 commands are 8-line templated files pointing to skills/SKILL.md via `@` reference. Edits to skill files propagate live without command re-generation.

### Install script (install.sh)

Generates command wrappers and creates symlinks for live propagation during local-dev:
1. `~/.claude/commands/shape/<name>.md` wrappers
2. `~/.claude/skills/shape-<name>` symlinks
3. Prunes stale principle-file `@` refs from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
4. Installs SessionStart hook into settings.json

**Idempotent**: Safe to re-run after `git pull`.

### Benchmarking infrastructure (docs/benchmarks.md, skills/plan-review-workspace/)

**plan-review calibration**: 5-scenario eval set, blinded grading, n=3 per cell

| Scenario | With-skill | Without-skill | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| (n=3 runs each) | ~93% | ~19% | +0.74 |

**Iterations tracked**: 5 iterations with token cost analysis, grader-prompt refinements

**Methodology documented**: For reuse on other skills (on roadmap)

## RAW FINDINGS FOR SYNTHESIS

1. **Coverage is front-heavy**: All 14 skills plus sub-agent sit in Define/Plan/Decide/Review/Verify/Ship phases (idea → spec → plan → PR prep). Zero coverage of build, deploy, or post-launch. **Intentional scoping per README; intended pairing with `addyosmani/agent-skills`.**

2. **Three skills exceed 300-line target** (plan-review 369, initiative-shape 310, roadmap-shape 303). All three are load-bearing and compress efficiently; no redundancy found. No splits recommended.

3. **Tracker-agnosticism is enforced at architecture level**: initiative-shape (the heaviest skill) checks at runtime whether a tracker binding is present; emits markdown or hands off to Workflow pack. **Zero coupling to Linear or other specific tracker in skill code.**

4. **Single agent file** (code-reviewer, 131 lines) provides pre-commit multi-axis review. No skill dispatches agents; agents are loaded by Workflow pack governance. **Agent design is sound: posture defined, context pre-loaded before seeing diff, model tier justified (Frontier = orchestrator).**

5. **Hooks are deterministic and mechanical** (2 total; 165 lines): PR signal-suppression detection, commit-time task annotation counting. No false positives by design.

6. **Execution capabilities are minimal by scope**: pr-prepare (context writing), verify-implementation (AC gate), code-reviewer (review before merge). No build/debug/deploy coverage. **This is intentional; README explicitly frames Shaper as Define/Plan/Design/Review, delegating Build/Ship/Deploy to execution pack.**

7. **Principle embedding is heavy**: Most skills embed 6–10+ principles as red flags, rationalisation rebuttals, gates. Only 3 standalone artefacts exist (PRODUCT_RULES, eng-principles-universal, eng-principles-agentic). **Follows authoring-learnings.md heuristic: a principle earns standalone artefact only when it has workflow + verifiable failure mode + agent reason to miss it.**

8. **References are well-organized and cited**: 10 reference files total (1,196 lines). No duplication of reference material within skills.

9. **SessionStart hook is elegant**: Loads meta-skill on every session; agent learns task routing from skill discovery flowchart. No push of all rules at session start.

10. **Frontmatter discipline is strict**: All 14 skills + 1 agent + 2 hooks have complete frontmatter with predecessor/relation declarations. Traceability is durable.

> DEVELOPER

do you think drain-cycle should be re-scoped? ideally the skills have sub-agents in them, but what i like about what drain-cycle can do is that it can delegate entirely to a different model (eg codex/chatgpt or even to kimi/deepseek).

> AGENT

Yes — I think drain-cycle should be re-scoped, and the cross-model point is exactly why. Here's my read:

**The split that makes sense: drain-cycle owns *processes*, Shaper owns *workflow*.**

Claude Code sub-agents (the Agent tool) can only ever spawn Claude models. drain-cycle spawns whole CLI processes — today `claude -p`, tomorrow `codex exec` or a kimi/deepseek wrapper. Those are different layers, and right now drain-cycle blurs them: its prompt template hardcodes the intra-issue workflow ("run /code-review-and-quality, fix findings, commit, push, mark Done"). That workflow prose is exactly what should live in skills instead.

Re-scoped, drain-cycle keeps only what a process-level supervisor can uniquely do: cycle selection and topological ordering, worktree setup, **vendor-agnostic worker spawning**, token/time/cost guardrails with SIGKILL, halt/resume, run logs and grading. Its prompt shrinks to roughly "you are working issue X in worktree Y; follow `/ship:work`" — one skill reference instead of an inlined procedure. That makes the workflow versionable in the pack, testable interactively, and identical whether you or a worker runs it.

**The sub-agent wrinkle your question exposes:** if a skill says "dispatch the security-auditor sub-agent," that step only executes on Claude Code. A codex or kimi worker can't run it. The fix is how superpowers structures it — personas live as standalone prompt files (`agents/security-auditor.md` is a role prompt + output contract, not Claude-specific machinery), and the skill defines the *step* ("get an adversarial security review of the diff; output format Z") with two bindings: Agent-tool dispatch when available, inline-sequential self-review with the same persona prompt when not. Same artefact, degraded gracefully.

**And the cross-model delegation gets *more* interesting, not less:** once drain-cycle is a vendor-agnostic spawner, it can spawn *reviewer* processes too — Claude implements, codex adversarially reviews, or vice versa. Genuinely-different-model review is a stronger correctness signal than same-model-different-prompt review, which is directly your stated purpose. Sub-agents in skills give you cheap same-session fan-out; drain-cycle gives you expensive cross-vendor adversarial passes for hard tickets. Both, different tiers.

So my answer to the question you paused: **both** — reviewer personas as portable prompt files that skills bind to sub-agents when on Claude Code, *and* drain-cycle re-scoped thinner so cross-model workers can follow the same skills.

2	name: initiative-types
3	description: >
4	  Six-type taxonomy for classifying a Linear initiative by what success means for it.
5	  Used by /initiative-shape to set the Objective shape and the rubric the KRs are judged

11	---
12	
13	# Initiative types (6)
14	
15	The `/initiative-shape` skill probes the project type before shaping KRs. The type determines what "success" means for the initiative: a methodology skill pack and a personal product can both pass cycle close, but they pass on different KRs, because their theories of success are different. Naming the type up front lets the skill load the right Objective shape and verification rubric — and lets a downstream agent reading the Linear project description apply the right rubric without re-deriving the taxonomy.
16	
17	The six types below are the ones actually observed across this portfolio (`agent-skills-shaper`, `nestl`, `agent-skills`, paused `em-os`, `stock-review`) plus one anticipated type (production / customer-facing). If a new initiative doesn't fit any of the six, the taxonomy needs updating — flag rather than force-fit.
18	
19	Each type's default KR mix is annotated with a **Role split** — which KR is the **bet** (the push), which are **brakes** (don't-regress guardrails), and which is **foundation** (instrumentation that makes the bet measurable). The role tags appended to each KR bullet (e.g. `· bet`, `· brake`, `· foundation`) sit alongside the leading/lagging and committed/aspirational descriptors. Roles are defined in `references/kr-quality-templates.md` "Roles within an initiative"; the splits below are defaults, not mandates.
20	
21	**Worked-example convention.** Each example below uses the PM-readable KR shape `/initiative-shape` emits — `(commit)` / `(stretch)` tags with `baseline` / `target` / `measured over` / `how we'll know` sub-fields. The examples model KR *content* and the per-type dimension mix; the rubric trace (the `*Layer 1 · Layer 2*` audit-footer under each KR and the `*Dimensions: …*` summary line) is added per the template in `skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md` and is left off here to keep the focus on phrasing.
22	
23	## Type 1 — Methodology skill pack
24	
25	*Examples: `agent-skills-shaper`, `agent-skills`.* Markdown-encoded decision rules invoked by humans or agents at decision moments. The consumer is the author plus any agent that loads the pack. The theory of success is that the skill fires at the right decision moment, and when it fires, decision quality improves. Authoring more skills is output, not outcome — invocation accuracy at the right moment, and the downstream quality of decisions made under the skill's guidance, are what count. Leading-indicator KRs measure invocation rate; lagging-indicator KRs measure decision quality when invoked.
26	
27	**Objective shape.** "For [agent or human invoker], make [decision moment] happen correctly without prompting." The Objective sentence names the *decision moment*, not the artefact. Authoring is implementation; what the OKR scores is whether the decision moment is now handled.
28	
29	**Default KR mix (3 KRs).** One leading + one lagging + one anti-output guard. Pair as two committed + one aspirational, or one committed + two aspirational, depending on which dimensions are inspectable today.
30	
31	**Role split (default).** The decision-quality KR is the **bet** (does the skill improve outcomes when it fires); the anti-output guard is a **brake** (the discipline must not regress at the bottleneck); the invocation-rate KR is **foundation** (without firing data the decision-quality KR can't be sampled). If invocation is already reliable, the invocation-rate KR reads as a brake instead — split foundation/brake to taste. These are defaults, not mandates.
32	
33	- **Invocation-rate KR (leading · foundation)** — does the skill fire at the right moment? Form: "[skill] fires (or is offered) in ≥X% of [decision-moment] across the next N cycles." Data sources: transcript history (`rtk discover`), Linear project list, sampled session logs. This is the leading indicator that the trigger description is well-targeted.
34	- **Decision-quality KR (lagging · bet)** — when it fires, does the outcome improve? Form: "in ≥X of last N sampled invocations, [skill] surfaced an issue or produced an artefact that would otherwise not have appeared." This is the lagging indicator that the skill body itself is well-authored.
35	- **Anti-output guard KR (committed · brake)** — the discipline holds at the bottleneck. Form: "zero [historically-common output failure] across [window]" (e.g., zero repo-aliased Linear projects, zero KRs without sub-fields). Catches drift between intent and practice.
36	
37	Adoption KRs ("skill installed in N repos") are output unless cross-repo adoption is itself the named goal — usually leave them out.
38	
39	**Worked example — `/initiative-shape` itself.**
40	
41	```
42	Goal:           For Anton (and any agent invoking Shaper), make
43	                initiatives properly shaped before they enter a cycle —
44	                so cycle planning works against goals and KRs rather than
45	                repo-aliased backlogs.
46	
47	KR1 (commit) — initiative-shape fires (or is offered) in ≥80% of
48	               new-initiative moments across the next 4 cycles
49	  baseline:        unknown — first cycle of measurement
50	  target:          ≥80% offered at new-initiative moments
51	  measured over:   next 4 cycles
52	  how we'll know:  transcript history (rtk discover), sampled
53	
54	KR2 (commit) — in ≥4 of last 5 created initiatives, all six fields
55	               pass the verification rubric
56	  baseline:        0/5 pass full rubric today
57	  target:          4/5 pass full rubric
58	  measured over:   next 4 cycles
59	  how we'll know:  Linear project descriptions, manual audit
60	
61	KR3 (stretch) — zero Linear projects created in the next 4 cycles
62	                that are repo-aliased rather than outcome-named
63	  baseline:        majority of historical projects repo-aliased
64	  target:          0 repo-aliased in window
65	  measured over:   next 4 cycles
66	  how we'll know:  Linear project list
67	
68	Kill condition: if KR2 isn't hit within 2 cycles of the skill update,
69	                the template is wrong rather than the operator
70	Project type:   1 — Methodology skill pack
71	```
72	
73	**Anti-patterns specific to Type 1.**
74	
75	- **"Author N new skills"** — output. Volume of skills is not what success means for a methodology pack. Success is the existing skills firing at the right moment with the right effect.
76	- **"Improve skill quality"** — unmeasurable; fails Wodtke's weekly-trackable test. Reshape into invocation-rate or decision-quality KRs with sample, target, and window.
77	- **"Update SKILL.md for X"** — task, not KR. Belongs on the issue body, not in the OKR.
78	- **"Skill installed in N repos"** — output disguised as outcome unless cross-repo spread is genuinely the named goal.
79	
80	**Verification rubric (Type 1).** A Type 1 KR is gradable if a fresh agent in the next session can name: (a) the data source for the sample (transcript history, Linear projects, session logs); (b) the sampling method (last-N, all-of-cycle, random); (c) the baseline — recorded, not "TBD"; (d) the target — numeric or binary, not "improved"; (e) a 0.0–1.0 grade at cycle close. If any of (a)–(e) is missing, the KR isn't gradable and cycle close degrades to a vibe check.
81	
82	## Type 2 — Personal product (single-user, running)
83	
84	*Example: `nestl` (Rails app).* Complete deployed software solving a recurring problem for one user. The consumer is the author as a single user. The theory of success is that the recurring job gets done reliably without manual intervention. Growth metrics, MAU, and adoption breadth are inapplicable — the dimensions that matter are correctness (zero false negatives or missed events), no-silent-failure (every failure surfaces in a visible alert within a bounded time), availability (scheduled jobs complete to SLO), and maintenance burden (zero manual restarts/redeploys over the observation window).
85	
86	**Objective shape.** "For [single user — name them], make [recurring job] happen reliably without manual intervention." The Objective names the *recurring job* being automated, not the technology stack or the feature set. Shipping more features is implementation; what the OKR scores is whether the recurring job now runs without nagging you.
87	
88	**Default KR mix (3 KRs).** One correctness (lagging) + one no-silent-failure (committed) + one maintenance-burden (committed). Where scheduled-job completion is the system's central guarantee, an availability KR may substitute for maintenance-burden, or sit alongside it as a 4th. Pair as one aspirational (correctness — the outcome) + two committed (operability — the brake). Adoption, retention, and growth KRs are categorically inapplicable to Type 2 — there is one user.
89	
90	**Role split (default).** Correctness is the **bet** (does the system get the right answer); maintenance-burden is the **brake** (don't regress into manual intervention); no-silent-failure is **foundation** (without surfaced failures you can't even tell whether the correctness bet held). An availability KR, when present, is a brake. These are defaults, not mandates.
91	
92	- **Correctness KR (lagging · bet)** — does the system get the right answer when it runs? Form: "≤X false negatives / missed events / wrong outputs across [N] runs in window" or "[result] matches [reference source] in ≥X% of [N] sampled runs." Data sources: production logs, sampled outputs against ground truth, the system's own audit trail. This is the lagging indicator that the implementation is sound.
93	- **No-silent-failure KR (committed · foundation)** — when a failure happens, do you find out? Form: "every error surfaces in [alert channel] within [bounded time] of failure" or "zero silent failures across [N] runs in window — every job either completes or fires an alert." Data sources: alert history, log diff between job runs and alert firings. This is the committed foundation — the observability that makes the correctness bet gradable, and a brake against silent failure: a Type 2 system that fails silently is worse than one that doesn't run at all, because you're now trusting an output that isn't there.
94	- **Maintenance-burden KR (committed · brake)** — does the human have to intervene to keep it running? Form: "zero manual restarts / redeploys / production-data hotfixes over [N-day window]" or "≤X manual interventions per [window]." Data sources: deploy history, ssh/console session log, on-call notes. This is the committed brake against the slow-leak failure mode where the product technically runs but consumes the operator's attention.
95	- **Availability KR (optional, committed when central · brake)** — do the scheduled jobs complete? Form: "scheduled job [name] completes within [time budget] in ≥X% of runs across [window]." Data sources: job scheduler logs, completion timestamps. Use when scheduled-job completion is the central guarantee; otherwise rolled into maintenance-burden.
96	
97	Feature-shipping KRs ("add [feature]", "build [integration]") are output. Growth KRs (DAU, MAU, retention, signups) are categorically inapplicable — there is one user.
98	
99	**Worked example — `nestl`-shaped personal Rails app, scheduled-job product.**
100	
101	```
102	Goal:           For Anton (single user), make the daily [recurring job]
103	                run reliably without manual intervention — so the output
104	                arrives on time without nagging the operator.
105	
106	KR1 (stretch) — ≤1 missed event / false negative per 30-day window
107	                across the daily run
108	  baseline:        unknown — first cycle of measurement
109	  target:          ≤1 missed event per 30 days
110	  measured over:   next 4 cycles (3 × 30-day observation windows)
111	  how we'll know:  production logs + sampled audit against source-of-truth
112	
113	KR2 (commit) — every job failure surfaces in [alert channel] within
114	               5 minutes; zero silent failures in window
115	  baseline:        unknown — first cycle of measurement
116	  target:          0 silent failures across 90 days
117	  measured over:   next 4 cycles
118	  how we'll know:  alert history vs job scheduler log diff
119	
120	KR3 (commit) — zero manual restarts, redeploys, or production-data
```

1	# KR quality templates — personal-project Layer 1 / Layer 2
2	
3	Reference cited by `skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md` Step 6.5 rules 5b and 5d. Use it when drafting key results to (a) pick a Layer 1 dimension and (b) shape the KR to its Layer 2 template.
4	
5	## Scope — personal projects only
6	
7	Every initiative in this workspace is a personal project: no production traffic, no real-user funnel, no on-call rotation. The vocabulary below is calibrated for that scale. Frameworks deliberately not imported as defaults:
8	
9	- **SRE SLO machinery** (availability / latency / error-budget). Assumes user traffic and an on-call team.
10	- **DORA four keys** (deployment frequency / lead time / change failure rate / MTTR). Assumes a deployment pipeline serving customers.
11	- **AARRR product funnels** (acquisition / activation / retention / referral / revenue). Assumes a multi-user product.
12	
13	A single initiative can still cite one of these — but only when the initiative genuinely has that property. They are not the default Layer 1 vocabulary, and a KR drawn from them must justify why the default four don't fit.
14	
15	## Layer 1 — the four dimensions
16	
17	| Dimension | What it answers | When it's load-bearing |
18	| -- | -- | -- |
19	| **Correctness** | does the thing produce the intended output on the cases I care about | always, for any build |
20	| **Outcome / behaviour change** | does the thing I built actually change what I do or how I work | most product-shaped initiatives (Types 2, 4, 5, 6 from `references/initiative-types.md`) |
21	| **Maintenance / future-me cost** | can I come back in 30 days and still navigate this | always — solo means future-me pays the whole tax |
22	| **Discipline / completion** | did the artefacts get finished, or did this half-ship | always — solo means nobody else will finish it |
23	
24	The four are deliberately distinct: correctness is about the artefact's output on inputs; outcome is about whether the artefact changes operator behaviour downstream; maintenance is about cost-of-future-edit; discipline is about whether the build actually completed. A KR that conflates two of them (e.g. "the skill works and I've used it 5 times") is a filler signal — pick one dimension per KR.
25	
26	## Layer 2 — measurement templates
27	
28	One template per Layer 1 dimension. Every template is verifiable by one person, locally, without instrumentation.
29	
30	### Correctness — Golden-path test
31	
32	**When it applies:** any initiative that produces a concrete artefact (skill, script, report, doc, configured tool) with verifiable output for known inputs.
33	
34	**Required fields:**
35	- named input(s) — specific fixtures, sample tickers, sample prompts, etc.
36	- named expected output — what "correct" looks like for each input
37	- grader — one-sentence describable command that runs the inputs and diffs against expected output (exit code + diff summary)
38	- judged-by date — when the check is run
39	
40	**Good example:**
41	> "Run `/initiative-shape` against the 5 fixture inputs in `fixtures/initiative-drafts/`; all 5 produce the 6-field structure verified by `diff` against checked-in expected outputs in `fixtures/initiative-drafts/expected/`; judged at cycle close."
42	> - baseline: `0/5` pass (fixtures don't exist yet — first issue creates them)
43	> - target: `5/5` pass
44	> - measured over: cycle close
45	> - how we'll know: `bin/grade-initiative-shape fixtures/initiative-drafts/` runs each fixture, diffs against `fixtures/initiative-drafts/expected/<name>.md`, exits 0 only if all pass; exit code + diff output cached at `fixtures/initiative-drafts/_runs/<cycle-id>.log`
46	
47	**Bad example:**
48	> "The skill works well."
49	> *(no named inputs, no named outputs, no verification method, no date — not gradable.)*
50	
51	### Outcome / behaviour change — Self-trial protocol
52	
53	**When it applies:** any initiative whose success is "this changes what I do or how I work" — methodology skills, productivity changes, decision-support tooling.
54	
55	**Required fields:**
56	- the situation (X) where the behaviour change should occur
57	- the next N occurrences over which it's judged (N is small — typically 3–10 — so the cycle window can contain it)
58	- the observable behaviour (Y) that confirms or denies the change
59	- grader — one-sentence describable command that scans the artefacts produced across N occurrences and emits a numeric grade or pass/fail
60	
61	**Good example:**
62	> "Next 5 initiatives shaped with `/initiative-shape` after this lands: zero filler KRs in the created Linear projects, graded by `bin/grade-kr-quality` against rules 5a–5f."
63	> - baseline: filler-KR rate is `~1 in 3` historically (eyeball estimate from past 9 projects)
64	> - target: `0/5` filler KRs
65	> - measured over: next 5 invocations
66	> - how we'll know: `bin/grade-kr-quality $(linear-project-list --since=cycle-start)` reads each project description and emits a per-project pass/fail across 5a–5f; the KR passes if total filler-KR count is 0; output cached at `~/.initiative-shape/grades/cycle-<id>.log`
67	
68	**Bad example:**
69	> "Initiatives will be better shaped."
70	> *(no situation, no N, no observable behaviour, no inspection method.)*
71	
72	### Maintenance / future-me cost — Structural cap + revisit gate
73	
74	**When it applies:** any initiative producing artefacts that will be edited or re-read after a delay — skills, references, code, docs.
75	
76	**Required fields:**
77	- size/shape cap — a stated bound: LOC, line count, section count, file count, function count
78	- revisit gate — a check at N days that the artefact is still navigable (typical: "I can answer question X from memory" or "I can find section Y without re-reading the whole file")
79	- grader — one-sentence describable structural-cap check using shell primitives (`wc -l`, `grep -c`, file count); the navigation gate is the manual half and is captured in a retro note
80	- judged-by date — when the revisit check is run
81	
82	**Good example:**
83	> "`skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md` stays ≤ 320 lines; in 30 days from cycle close I can locate where rule 5c lives without grepping."
84	> - baseline: 281 lines today
85	> - target: ≤ 320 lines, navigation check passes
86	> - measured over: 30 days from cycle close
87	> - how we'll know: `wc -l skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md` returns ≤ 320 (cap check, automated); the 30-day navigation check is the manual half — captured in a one-paragraph retro note in `retros/<cycle-id>.md`
88	
89	**Bad example:**
90	> "The skill stays maintainable."
91	> *(no cap, no revisit gate, no date — vibe.)*
92	
93	### Discipline / completion — Artefact-exists + sections-complete
94	
95	**When it applies:** any initiative whose risk is half-shipping — the build started but the doc / test / reference / cleanup didn't land.
96	
97	**Required fields:**
98	- named artefact (file path)
99	- named sections within the artefact (e.g. "rule 5 has 5a/5b/5c/5d/5e populated", "rationalisations table has the new row")
100	- grader — one-sentence describable existence + section-count + no-placeholder check (chained shell primitives: `test -f`, `grep -c '^### '`, `! grep -E 'TBD|unknown'`)
101	- zero placeholders — no `TBD`, no `unknown`, no `we'll figure it out`
102	- predecessor / supersedes declaration if the artefact replaces an earlier one
103	
104	**Good example:**
105	> "ABA-191 closes only after `skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md` has rule 5 enumerated as 5a/5b/5c/5d/5e each with a 1-line pass condition, rule 6 has the extended placeholder ban list and concrete-artefact requirement, the rationalisations table has the 'padding to 3' row, and `references/kr-quality-templates.md` exists with all four templates."
106	> - baseline: rule 5 is one row, rule 6 has the short ban list, no kr-quality-templates reference
107	> - target: all four artefact changes landed
108	> - measured over: cycle close
109	> - how we'll know: `test -f references/kr-quality-templates.md && [ $(grep -cE '^\| 5[a-f] \|' skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md) -ge 5 ] && ! grep -nE 'TBD|currently unknown|the logs|the system' skills/initiative-shape/SKILL.md references/kr-quality-templates.md` — exit code + matched-line output
110	
111	**Bad example:**
112	> "The work will be documented."
113	> *(no artefact path, no sections named, no completion definition.)*
114	
115	## Pattern for a 3-KR draft
116	
117	A clean 3-KR draft typically picks 3 of the 4 dimensions, not 3 of the same one. Some patterns by initiative type:
118	
119	- **Type 1 methodology skill pack** — outcome (invocation behaviour) + correctness (per-invocation decision quality) + discipline (artefact completion).
120	- **Type 2 personal product** — correctness (named-fixture output) + outcome (does it change my workflow) + maintenance (future-me cost).
```

13	
14	# HTML skeleton
15	
16	The render-html skill wraps every markdown body in the shell below. The shell is the **only** mechanism by which output styling and navigation arrive — no external CSS, no external JS, no remote images. That rule is load-bearing for the skill's "opens via `file://` with no network" guarantee; reviewers attach these files to emails and store them in private wikis where CDN URLs silently break.
17	
18	The visual language is **product-UI**: Inter (system fallback), tight type, indigo accent, sidebar with numbered nav and scrollspy, status pills and metadata grids as first-class. Reads as a Linear/Stripe spec page rather than a markdown previewer. Pattern treatments (P1–P12) extend this language; they don't introduce a competing one.
19	
20	## The hard rule
21	
22	Anything injected into the rendered output must satisfy all three:
23	
24	- **No `<link rel="stylesheet">`.** All CSS lives in the inline `<style>` block.
25	- **No `<script src=...>`.** All JS lives in the inline `<script>` block at the end of `<body>`.
26	- **No remote `<img>` URLs.** Inline SVG is preferred; base64 data URIs are allowed when an SVG is impractical. Remote URLs (`http:`, `https:`, protocol-relative `//`) are not.
27	
28	If a future pattern needs richer interactivity (charts, diagrams, syntax highlighting), inline the minimal library or hand-write the SVG. Adding a CDN is not an option.
29	
30	## Substitution tokens
31	
32	| Token | Source | Notes |
33	|---|---|---|
34	| `{{title}}` | The source markdown's first H1 | Goes in both `<title>` and the page `<h1>`. |
35	| `{{breadcrumb}}` | Inferred from path (e.g. `docs/adr/001-...` → `Architecture · ADRs · ADR-001`) or empty | Optional; render empty `<div>` if nothing meaningful to show. |
36	| `{{header-pills}}` | Status pill (P10) + identifier pill + date pill, in that order | Rendered into the `.pill-row` slot. Empty if none apply. |
37	| `{{meta-grid}}` | Definition-list rows for `Source`, `Rendered`, plus any frontmatter fields after P9 lifts them | The grid is always rendered; if only `Source` and `Rendered` apply, it shows two rows. |
38	| `{{toc-entries}}` | One `<li>` per H2 (and indented H3), with anchor href to the heading's slug | H1 is the title, not a TOC entry. Slugs are kebab-case, deduplicated `-2`, `-3`. |
39	| `{{status-block}}` | One-line aside under "Status" kicker in the sidebar (e.g. "Accepted 31 Mar 2026. No superseding ADR.") | Empty `<div>` if no status info. |
40	| `{{body-html}}` | The markdown body converted to HTML, with H2/H3 carrying `id="<slug>"` and wrapped per `html-patterns.md` | Pattern markup substitutes here. |
41	| `{{source-path}}` | Path of the input `.md` file, relative to the repo root if possible | Shown in the metadata grid and footer. |
42	| `{{render-date}}` | ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD) of the render | Provenance only — re-renders on the same day produce no diff. |
43

219	      <h1>{{title}}</h1>
220	      <div class="pill-row">{{header-pills}}</div>
221	      <dl class="meta-grid">{{meta-grid}}</dl>
222	    </div>

224	    {{body-html}}

228	</div>
229	
230	<script>
231	  // Scrollspy: highlight the TOC entry for the section currently in view.
232	  const links = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('aside nav a'));
233	  const targets = links.map(a => document.getElementById(a.getAttribute('href').slice(1))).filter(Boolean);
234	  const byId = new Map(targets.map((el, i) => [el.id, links[i]]));
235	  const io = new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
236	    for (const e of entries) {
237	      if (e.isIntersecting) {
238	        links.forEach(a => a.classList.remove('active'));
239	        byId.get(e.target.id)?.classList.add('active');
240	      }
241	    }
242	  }, { rootMargin: '-30% 0px -60% 0px' });
243	  targets.forEach(t => io.observe(t));
244	</script>
245	</body>
246	</html>

248	
249	## Design notes
250	
251	- **Inter via system fallback** — the font stack starts with `"Inter"` for environments where it's installed; otherwise falls back to `ui-sans-serif` / `system-ui`. The `font-feature-settings` lines (`cv11`, `ss01`, `ss03`) activate Inter's curly-l, single-storey-a, and rounded variants when Inter is present; they're harmless no-ops otherwise. **No web-font load** — that would violate the hard rule.
252	- **Indigo accent** — `#5b4cff` (light) / `#8b7cff` (dark). Used for active nav, links, decision callouts (via P3), and primary card borders on hover. Soft variant `--accent-soft` for fills.
253	- **Semantic colour tokens** — `--ok`, `--warn`, `--info`, `--danger`, each with a soft companion for low-contrast fills. Pills, callouts, and chips draw from this palette consistently; pattern authors should not introduce ad-hoc hex values.
254	- **Sidebar is the primary nav** — 260px sticky column, numbered entries (`01`, `02`, …), scrollspy-highlighted. Brand block at the top is the doc family ("Nestl · ADRs", "PDE · Roadmap"). Status block at the bottom is the one-line state line.
255	- **Doc head is structured** — breadcrumbs, H1, pill row, metadata grid. Even minimal docs show source + render date in the metadata grid, so provenance is always visible without footer-hunting.
256	- **Section headers carry index + h2** — every body section wraps in `<section class="s"><header><span class="ix">01</span><h2>…</h2></header>…</section>`. Patterns that attach colour tags (P3) append a `.tag` span inside the `<h2>`.
257	- **Prose defaults are styled** — even a section that matches no pattern still gets readable type, table styling, blockquote, pre/code treatment. The fallback is "well-typeset doc," not "raw HTML."
258	- **Print** — sidebar hidden, main expands. Reviewers print-to-PDF for offline annotation get usable output.
259	- **Responsive** — below 880px the sidebar collapses above the body and nav becomes a horizontal pill list. Skill is desktop-first but mobile shouldn't be broken.
260	- **Dark mode** — `prefers-color-scheme: dark` swaps every variable. No toggle UI (out of scope).
261	
262	## When pattern treatments arrive
263	
264	Pattern markup substitutes into `{{body-html}}` — the shell itself does not change. Pattern CSS appends to the inline `<style>` block via additions, not replacements. Every pattern class is prefixed `p-`; the shell uses no `p-` classes, so collisions are impossible. The fallback (well-typeset prose with index + h2) is the default for any section the catalogue doesn't classify.
265
